Business archetype: East African local-food restaurant (no Western course structure)
Category families used: FAM-R01; FAM-R02; FAM-R03; FAM-R04; FAM-R05; FAM-R06; FAM-R07; FAM-R08; FAM-11; FAM-39
Representative observed categories and i: Flat priced lines with no starter, main or dessert sections: ugali, brochettes, inyamo n'ibirayi, urukwavu (grilled rabbit), inkoko, isambaza, isombe, pasta with dried meat; isombe also sold by weight
Combos, bundles and modifiers: No structured combos observed; family-style sharing is the norm rather than a priced bundle
Item reuse and placement: Few placements per item; sharing culture means placement matters less than portion controls
Notes on applying the model: This is the archetype the Western template fails. Categories must come from the regional set. The staple is a category, not a side. Weight-based variants must be modelled (TAG-58).

Business archetype: Multi-location cafe chain (restaurant, grocery, deli and wine cellar under one brand)
Named menus: Breakfast menu; Coffee and pastries; Grab and go; Grocery retail
Category families used: FAM-17; FAM-27; FAM-29; FAM-31; FAM-32; FAM-20; FAM-01; FAM-23; FAM-26; FAM-34; FAM-36
Representative observed categories and i: A category set published identically across six branches: pastries and sweets; breads; cakes; hot and iced teas; hot and iced coffees; breakfast; starters and sharing
Combos, bundles and modifiers: Pastry selection box defined as choose four; single coffee and pastry combination restricted to a time window
Item reuse and placement: Items shared across all branches; formats diverge by branch without changing the category set
Notes on applying the model: Direct evidence that central category standardisation with local format divergence is achievable. The choose-four box is a composite item whose components are existing items. The time-windowed combination is a combo plus an availability window.
Evidence basis: Observed published category set across branches, October 2026

Representative observed categories and i: Italian menu with bread, nibbles, salads, soups, risottos, a house-branded pasta heading, pizza, mains and dolci, using a coded multi-letter dietary and allergen notation on items and modifiers; lounge menu with wings, samosa, spring roll, club and Philly sandwiches, mishkaki with kachumbari, glazed pork ribs with kachumbari and noodles, jollof rice, South Indian curry, butter chicken, bibimbap; buffet offering; brunch set composed from component selections
Combos, bundles and modifiers: Add-tin and other supplements attached to menu items; buffet trays not individually priced; set menus priced by course count

Notes on applying the model: The archetype that most needs all seven dimensions. Buffet, banquet and priced set menus are menu types, not categories. Coded notation must be rendered as structured values, not free text, and the decoded legend belongs with the business.

Representative observed categories and i: Signature or house cocktails; classics; beer split into draught and packaged; wine by the glass and by the bottle; spirits by base; low and no-alcohol; snack and small-plate food
Combos, bundles and modifiers: Flight of three; spirit poured neat or with mixer; house spritz variants
Item reuse and placement: Shared classics list; the food list is a second named menu on the same collection
Notes on applying the model: In East African markets the beer family must additionally split lager, malt and non-alcoholic, and traditional fermented drinks must be representable. Alcohol content (TAG-46) drives age-restriction logic and cannot be inferred from the family.
Evidence basis: Industry practice, converging across independent operator guidance

Category families used: FAM-R07; FAM-R08; FAM-R09; FAM-R10; FAM-R11; FAM-R12; FAM-R01; FAM-R02; FAM-R03; FAM-R14; FAM-R18; FAM-19; FAM-18; FAM-13; FAM-23; FAM-26; FAM-32; FAM-33; FAM-34; FAM-35
Representative observed categories and i: Compact menu built around the fastest-moving cooked items; cuisine presented as a discovery facet rather than as a category
Combos, bundles and modifiers: High modifier density for spice level, portion and add-ons; bundles used to lift average order value
Item reuse and placement: Every item must be orderable through the delivery channel only; service format (TAG-51) is therefore constant
Notes on applying the model: This archetype is governed by delivery-platform constraints: two-level grouping, category-level hours disallowed, pickup versus delivery pricing, and a fixed attribute vocabulary. PEWA should generate the platform surface from the same items rather than maintaining a second menu.
Evidence basis: Platform documentation and observed delivery guidance

Business archetype: Business offering combos and configurable meals
Named menus: A la carte; Combo menu; Set menu
Menu types: A la carte; Bundle pricing; Prix fixe; Table d'hote
Category families used: Any family; combos are items and are deliberately NOT a category family
Representative observed categories and i: Modular build-your-own offering with choose-any-N grills, choose-N pastry boxes, breakfast set compositions and priced party sets
Combos, bundles and modifiers: Composite item whose components are existing items; component choice constraints; fixed-price set drawn from named categories
Item reuse and placement: The same component item participates in many composites and remains a single item in the catalogue
Notes on applying the model: Combos must never become a category. Modelling them as items with component references is what allows a business to change a combo price without touching any component item.
Evidence basis: Observed combo and set-menu patterns across markets
